annotations.keyFindings: In 412 older adults, weekly reminders and a call after missed weeks raised attendance at two thirds of sessions from 41 to 54 percent over 24 weeks; falls over 12 months did not differ.
annotations.limitations: Unblinded; instructors aware of allocation; falls self-reported.

annotations.keyFindings: Peer volunteer calls were associated with home exercise on three or more days a week in 62 against 35 percent; class attendance similar.
annotations.limitations: Non-random programme comparison; self-reported diaries; older population in the comparison programme.

claims.text: With weekly reminders and a call after missed weeks, attendance at two thirds or more of sessions over 24 weeks was 54 percent with support and 41 percent with usual classes.
claims.passage: Attendance at two thirds or more of sessions over 24 weeks was 54 percent with support and 41 percent with usual classes.
claims.interpretation: Planning values for the primary outcome; the local baseline of 38 percent is similar.

claims.text: Home exercise diaries were completed on at least three days a week by 62 percent of participants who received peer calls and 35 percent of those who did not.
claims.passage: Home exercise diaries were completed on at least three days a week by 62 percent of participants who received peer calls and 35 percent of those who did not.
claims.interpretation: Peer calls may help home exercise more than attendance; a secondary outcome.

claims.text: Falls over 12 months did not differ between groups (rate ratio 0.94, 95 percent CI 0.71 to 1.25).
claims.passage: Falls over 12 months did not differ between groups (rate ratio 0.94, 95 percent CI 0.71 to 1.25).
claims.interpretation: Falls are not a feasible primary outcome at this scale.

synthesis: Two retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; the five earlier items remain unverified leads and are not part of the certainty. One trial found that reminders and calls after missed weeks raised attendance from 41 to 54 percent without a detectable effect on falls, and a non-random comparison linked peer volunteer calls with more home exercise. The evidence is thin but directly relevant, and it supports attendance as the primary outcome with home exercise as secondary and falls reported descriptively.
gradeRationale: Two studies only, one unblinded trial and one non-random comparison; consistent direction but imprecise and indirect for peer calls.
summary: Two records appraised; three claims; certainty low over the retrieved records only.
